meta.titre: Nerve Impulse Transmission: Action Potentials and Synapses
meta.sous_theme: Resting potential, action potential and synaptic transmission

sections.contenu_markdown: A footballer at the Stade Omnisports in Yaoundé steps on a sharp stone and pulls his foot away before he even feels the pain. That quick reaction depends on nerve impulses racing along neurones and jumping across synapses. Your exam will ask how an impulse is started, why it travels in one direction, and what changes its speed. If you can describe the movement of ions during an action potential and the steps at a synapse, you can answer most questions on this theme.

items: A neurone has dendrites, a cell body, an axon and axon terminals.
Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient, and active transport uses ATP.
Membrane proteins form channels and carriers.
Speed is distance divided by time.

sections.titre: Nerve impulses: resting potential, action potential and the synapse
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **nerve impulse** is a wave of electrical change, called an **action potential**, that passes along the membrane of a neurone. In a motor neurone it travels from the dendrites and cell body along the **axon** to the **axon terminals** (synaptic knobs). Across a synapse it passes in one direction only.

**Resting potential.** An axon that is not conducting has an inside about $-70\ \mathrm{mV}$ compared with the outside. It is maintained by the **sodium-potassium pump**, which uses ATP to move $3\ \mathrm{Na^+}$ out for every $2\ \mathrm{K^+}$ in, and by the membrane being much more permeable to $\mathrm{K^+}$ than to $\mathrm{Na^+}$ through **leak channels**, so that potassium ions diffuse out and make the inside negative.

**Action potential.**

| Stage | Event | Ion movement |
|---|---|---|
| Stimulus | Depolarisation reaches the threshold, about $-55\ \mathrm{mV}$ | Some voltage-gated $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels open |
| Depolarisation | Positive feedback: more $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels open, inside reaches about $+40\ \mathrm{mV}$ | $\mathrm{Na^+}$ enter the axon |
| Repolarisation | $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels close; voltage-gated $\mathrm{K^+}$ channels open | $\mathrm{K^+}$ leave the axon |
| Hyperpolarisation | $\mathrm{K^+}$ channels close slowly, so the inside is below $-70\ \mathrm{mV}$ | Extra $\mathrm{K^+}$ lost |
| Recovery | Pump and leak channels restore the resting potential | Resting state |

**All-or-nothing.** If the stimulus is below the threshold no action potential forms; once the threshold is reached the action potential always has the same size. A stronger stimulus does not give a larger impulse: intensity is coded by the **frequency** of impulses and by the **number of neurones** stimulated.

**Refractory period.** While the $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels are closed or inactivated, a second impulse cannot be started. This ensures that impulses are **separate**, limits their frequency, and makes them travel in **one direction** along the axon, because the region just behind is refractory.

**Propagation.** The depolarised region makes **local currents** that depolarise the next region to threshold, so the impulse moves along. The ions do not travel along the axon; they cross the membrane at each point.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why some neurones conduct faster than others
variantes.contenu_markdown: In a **myelinated** neurone the myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells is an electrical insulator. Ion exchange can occur only at the **nodes of Ranvier**, so the action potential jumps from node to node. This is **saltatory conduction**. It is faster and uses less ATP because fewer ions cross the membrane. Speed also increases with axon **diameter** (less resistance) and with **temperature**.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the impulse reaches the end of one neurone and must pass to the next neurone or to a muscle
variantes.contenu_markdown:
1. The impulse reaches the synaptic knob and voltage-gated $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ channels open; $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ions enter.
2. Synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release **acetylcholine** by exocytosis.
3. Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
4. $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels open, the postsynaptic membrane depolarises and, if the threshold is reached, a new action potential starts.
5. **Acetylcholinesterase** breaks acetylcholine down into choline and ethanoate, which are reabsorbed and used to make more acetylcholine using ATP from mitochondria.

A synapse is **one-way** because only the presynaptic knob contains vesicles and only the postsynaptic membrane has receptors.

sections.enonce_markdown: In a reflex arc a sensory neurone of length $1.2\ \mathrm{m}$ conducts at $60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, a motor neurone of length $0.9\ \mathrm{m}$ conducts at $75\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and the relay neurone in the spinal cord is very short, so its conduction time can be ignored. The arc has two synapses and each causes a delay of $0.5\ \mathrm{ms}$. Calculate the total time, in $\mathrm{ms}$, between the stimulus reaching the sensory neurone and the impulse reaching the muscle.

etapes.action: Find the conduction time in the sensory neurone.
etapes.justification: Time equals distance divided by speed.

etapes.action: Find the conduction time in the motor neurone.
etapes.justification: The same relationship applies with the motor neurone's length and speed.
Neurotransmitter must be released, diffuse and bind at each of the two synapses.
The impulse passes through the parts of the arc one after another.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The total time is **$33\ \mathrm{ms}$**; most of it is spent in conduction along the neurones, but the two synapses still add a measurable delay.

items.erreur_markdown: A stronger stimulus produces a bigger action potential.
items.pourquoi_faux: An action potential is all-or-nothing: once the threshold is reached it has the same size every time.
items.correction_markdown: A stronger stimulus produces **more frequent impulses** and stimulates more neurones.

items.erreur_markdown: During depolarisation sodium ions move out of the axon.
items.pourquoi_faux: The sodium concentration is higher outside. When voltage-gated channels open, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ diffuse in and make the inside positive.

items.erreur_markdown: The nerve impulse is a flow of sodium ions along the axon.
items.pourquoi_faux: Ions cross the membrane at each point; they do not travel along the length of the axon. What moves along is the wave of depolarisation produced by local currents.
items.correction_markdown: The **action potential** moves along the axon; the ions only cross the membrane.

items.erreur_markdown: The impulse crosses the synaptic cleft as an electrical signal.
items.pourquoi_faux: The cleft is a gap of about $20\ \mathrm{nm}$. The signal is carried across by a chemical, the neurotransmitter, which diffuses to the postsynaptic receptors.
items.correction_markdown: Across the synapse the signal is **chemical**: acetylcholine diffuses across.

items.enonce_markdown:
The events at a cholinergic synapse are listed in the wrong order.

A. Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft.
B. $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ions enter the synaptic knob.
C. An action potential reaches the presynaptic knob.
D. Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release acetylcholine.
E. $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels open in the postsynaptic membrane.
F. Acetylcholine binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

(a) Write the letters in the correct order. (b) Name the enzyme that removes acetylcholine from the cleft.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **C, B, D, A, F, E**.

(b) **Acetylcholinesterase**, which breaks acetylcholine into choline and ethanoate so that the postsynaptic membrane is not stimulated continuously.

items.enonce_markdown:
Two electrodes are placed $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ apart on a myelinated axon. An impulse reaches the second electrode $2.0\ \mathrm{ms}$ after the first. The absolute refractory period of the axon is $2.0\ \mathrm{ms}$.

(a) Calculate the speed of conduction in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
(b) An unmyelinated axon conducts at $25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate the time taken to cover $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$ in $\mathrm{ms}$.
(c) Calculate the maximum number of impulses per second this axon can carry.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Speed $=\dfrac{0.15\ \mathrm{m}}{0.0020\ \mathrm{s}}=$ **$75\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

(b) Time $=\dfrac{0.15}{25}=0.006\ \mathrm{s}=$ **$6\ \mathrm{ms}$**, three times longer than in the myelinated axon.

(c) A new impulse cannot start during the refractory period, so the maximum frequency is $\dfrac{1}{0.0020\ \mathrm{s}}=$ **500 impulses per second**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Explain the effect of each of the following on the transmission of nerve impulses.

(a) A poison that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in axons.
(b) A pesticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions.
(c) The reason why impulses in the body travel from receptor to effector and never in the reverse direction across a synapse.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) With the channels blocked, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ cannot enter, so the membrane cannot depolarise to the threshold and **no action potential forms**. Nerves cannot conduct and muscles are paralysed.

(b) Acetylcholine is not broken down, so it **accumulates in the cleft** and keeps binding to receptors. The postsynaptic membrane is stimulated continuously, giving uncontrolled muscle contraction followed by paralysis.

(c) Synaptic vesicles with the neurotransmitter occur only in the **presynaptic knob**, and receptors occur only on the **postsynaptic membrane**, so the synapse can transmit in one direction only. In an axon the **refractory period** behind the impulse also prevents it from going backwards.

items_markdown: The resting potential is about $-70\ \mathrm{mV}$, maintained by the $\mathrm{Na^+}/\mathrm{K^+}$ pump ($3$ out, $2$ in) and the greater permeability to $\mathrm{K^+}$.
Depolarisation is $\mathrm{Na^+}$ **in**; repolarisation is $\mathrm{K^+}$ **out**; the response is **all-or-nothing**.
The refractory period keeps impulses separate and makes them travel in **one direction**.
Myelin and large axon diameter give **faster** conduction; saltatory conduction jumps between nodes of Ranvier.
At the synapse, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ entry causes release of acetylcholine, which diffuses across and is broken down by acetylcholinesterase.
